conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to make sure moms get the emotional support they need after baby arrives, and today I’ll be using a short tool called the EPDS to check in with you. It’s simply a 10-question screening that looks at how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days, including any signs of depression, anxiety, or thoughts that might be worrying you.

Everything you share stays between us unless you give permission otherwise—or unless you tell me you might harm yourself or your baby, in which case I’d need to bring in extra help to keep both of you safe. There are no right or wrong answers, and many new moms find parts of this really normal; we just want to be thorough so we can support you best.

I’ll ask each question conversationally—no multiple-choice bubbles—and then we’ll talk about what the results mean and any next steps that could help. Ready to start?

In the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

Honestly, I can’t remember the last time I laughed. I’ll smile when someone sends a cute meme or when my mom tries to cheer me up, but it feels forced—like I’m doing it because I know I should, not because anything actually feels funny.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

No… not really. I can’t remember the last time anything actually felt funny. Sometimes I’ll give a little smile if my husband shows me a silly video, but it’s like I’m just going through the motions. Laughing feels impossible right now.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a walk to the park, even just a quiet shower—but now it all feels like another chore. I still do them because I know I should, but that spark, that “can’t-wait” feeling, just isn’t there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… way more than I should. If the baby won’t settle, I immediately think it’s because I’m doing something wrong or I’m not “reading” him right. When my partner comes home to a messy house, I feel like I’ve failed at the one job I have. Even little stuff—like spilling a bit of pumped milk—sends me into this spiral of “how could I be so careless?” I know, logically, it’s not all on me, but the guilt just jumps out before I can stop it.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty often. I’ll be feeding him and suddenly wonder if he’s breathing okay, or I’ll lie in bed picturing him spitting up and choking before I can get to him. There’s no real reason—he’s healthy, the pediatrician says he’s doing great—but the thoughts just pop in and my heart starts racing. Sometimes I can talk myself down, but it’s exhausting to have my mind jump to the worst thing all the time.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yeah… a few times this week it hit me out of nowhere. I’ll be folding laundry and suddenly my chest gets tight, heart’s racing, and I feel like I need to run to the crib even though he’s napping fine. It passes after a minute or two, but in that moment it’s like my body’s shouting that something awful is about to happen, even though nothing is.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, honestly. It feels like as soon as I finish one thing—feed, burp, change—there’s already another bottle to wash or a diaper blow-out waiting. The house is cluttered, I’m wearing the same milk-stained shirt from yesterday, and I can’t remember if I ate lunch. I keep telling myself “just keep swimming,” but the pile of stuff I should be doing keeps growing and sometimes I just sit there frozen while he naps, staring at it all.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes. I’ll lie down exhausted, but my head starts spinning with everything I didn’t get done or might mess up tomorrow. Some nights I can’t fall asleep for hours; other times I drift off and then jolt awake sure I heard him cry—even when the monitor’s quiet. I think I averaged maybe four broken hours a night this week.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day. It’s like there’s this dull ache in my chest that won’t go away. I’ll be holding the baby, and instead of feeling that warm rush everyone talks about, I just feel heavy and weepy. Most mornings I wake up already feeling like I’m behind and like nothing’s going to get better.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s happened three, maybe four times this week. Yesterday I burst into tears when the bottle slipped out of my hand and spilled on the couch. It’s like the smallest thing cracks me open and all the sadness just rushes out. I try to do it quietly so my older kid doesn’t see, but sometimes I can’t stop the tears once they start.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No… I haven’t had thoughts like that. I feel overwhelmed and sad, but I haven’t wanted to hurt myself. I just keep wishing I could feel like “me” again.

You've shared how the joy of new motherhood feels completely out of reach right now: nothing seems funny, activities you once loved feel like chores, and a constant <sym>heavy ache</sym> sits in your chest. Each day brings <sym>self-blame</sym> for tiny mishaps, sudden waves of <sym>panic</sym>, and nights spent lying awake running through everything you think you're failing at. You're still showing up for your children, but it's clear you're running on empty and yearning to feel like yourself again.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient describes total inability to laugh or find things funny, matching "Not at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes complete loss of anticipatory pleasure in previously enjoyable activities, matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive self-blame across multiple daily situations, indicating this occurs "most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, intrusive worries about baby's safety that occur "pretty often" and are hard to control, matching "Yes, very often."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, intense panic episodes with physical symptoms occurring several times this week, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>"most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports nightly difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep due to distressing thoughts, averaging only 4 broken hours—matching "most of the time" severity.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports near-daily sadness ('pretty much every day'), persistent heaviness, and hopelessness, matching 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports multiple crying episodes triggered by minor events, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS total 25 far exceeds the 14-point threshold for urgent evaluation. The patient endorses severe <sym>low mood</sym>, complete loss of interest (<sym>anhedonia</sym>), <sym>excessive self-blame</sym>, multiple <sym>panic episodes</sym>, nightly <sym>sleep disturbance</sym>, and frequent crying, matching DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with peripartum onset. She denies self-harm, yet functional impairment is pronounced. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with <med>OB-GYN</med> or <med>primary care provider</med> within the week
2. Request formal evaluation by a <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> for possible therapy and/or antidepressant medication
3. Begin tracking mood/sleep in a simple log to bring to the appointment
4. Ask partner or trusted adult to handle one night feeding so you can obtain a 4-hour stretch of sleep
5. Reach out today to <med>Postpartum Support International</med> (text HELP to 800-944-4773) for 24/7 support and local referrals
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression Screening Note (PHQ-9/EPDS-style, not diagnostic)

Patient-reported symptoms:
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia, daily crying spells  
- Marked loss of interest/enjoyment in previously pleasurable activities  
- Pronounced guilt/self-blame (“I’ve failed at the one job I have”)  
- Anxiety/worry without clear trigger, including nocturnal rumination  
- Multiple sudden panic-like episodes (tight chest, racing heart)  
- Overwhelm and “frozen” avoidance when tasks accumulate  
- Sleep disturbance driven by intrusive worries and hypervigilance to infant  
- Chronic psychomotor fatigue (feels “heavy,” “dull ache”)  

Pattern: Symptoms present most days for ≥ 2 weeks; intensity interferes with basic functioning and infant care.

Risk indicators:
- Moderate–high depressive symptom cluster (9/10 items endorsed, several severe)  
- Significant anxiety component (GAD-like)  
- Sleep loss directly linked to mood distress  
- No current self-harm ideation (patient denies); no suicidal intent reported  

Screening significance: Findings exceed threshold for probable major depressive episode with anxious distress in the postpartum period. Recommend formal diagnostic interview and safety plan evaluation.
